content.text: Microservices aren't the modern default; they're a trade. You get firm module boundaries and independent deployment, and you pay with remote calls, eventual consistency and a lot of operational work, a cost Martin Fowler calls the Microservice Premium. Most new systems should start as a monolith with strong internal modules: it scales out behind a load balancer, and it lets you learn where the boundaries belong before you make them expensive to move.

A team of four starts a new booking product. Before the first customer signs up, the diagram already has eight services, a message broker, an API gateway and a Kubernetes cluster. Three months later, most features touch three repositories, and the most common production bug is one service shipping a contract change before the service that calls it. None of these pieces is wrong on its own. The team simply paid, on day one, for problems it didn't have yet.
The common misconception

The belief: microservices are how modern systems are built, and a monolith is legacy you'll eventually throw away because it can't scale. Starting with services, the thinking goes, saves a painful rewrite later.

It's easy to see why smart people believe it. The famous success stories are microservice stories. Microsoft's Azure guide lists real benefits: independent deployment, small focused teams, fault isolation and scaling each service on its own. And many developers have suffered a tangled monolith. Fowler observes that the Big Ball of Mud is the most common architectural pattern, and that frustration with what usually happens to monoliths is what drove several teams to microservices.
The half-truth: those benefits are real. But they come at a price, and two of the biggest reasons people give, scaling and modularity, don't actually require services.
What actually happens
Services come with a premium

Fowler's 2015 post puts it bluntly: microservices "introduce complexity on their own account. This adds a premium to a project's cost and risk - one that often gets projects into serious trouble." He lists what you take on: "automated deployment, monitoring, dealing with failure, eventual consistency, and other factors that a distributed system introduces." His
Microservice Premium
guideline follows: "don't even consider microservices unless you have a system that's too complex to manage as a monolith."

His trade-offs article spells out the costs. Distribution: "Distributed systems are harder to program, since remote calls are slow and are always at risk of failure." Operations: "You need a mature operations team to manage lots of services, which are being redeployed regularly." Microsoft's guide agrees: "Each service is simpler, but the entire system as a whole is more complex."
A monolith can scale

Lewis and Fowler's original microservices article states it plainly: "You can horizontally scale the monolith by running many instances behind a load-balancer." The real limitation is narrower: scaling a monolith means scaling the whole application, not only the part that needs more resources. That matters for some systems, but it's a specific problem, not a reason to start distributed. Continuous delivery doesn't require services either: Fowler cites Facebook and Etsy.
Boundaries are hardest to get right at the start
Services "only work well if you come up with good, stable boundaries between the services," Fowler writes in
MonolithFirst
, which is the job of finding the right
bounded contexts

. "Any refactoring of functionality between services is much harder than it is in a monolith. But even experienced architects working in familiar domains have great difficulty getting boundaries right at the beginning." In a monolith, a wrong boundary costs a refactoring. Between services, it costs a contract change, a data migration and a coordinated release.

That's why he reports a pattern: "Almost all the successful microservice stories have started with a monolith that got too big and was broken up", while almost every system he'd heard of that was built as microservices from scratch "has ended up in serious trouble."
What you need first is modularity

The benefit people actually want is strong module boundaries, and a monolith can have them. Fowler: "It's perfectly possible to have firm module boundaries with a monolith, but it requires discipline." That discipline is what makes a later split possible. A
modular monolith
is one deployable unit whose modules own their data and talk only through small public contracts.
The fix: modules with real boundaries

✅ Right

content.text: Ordering now calls
billing.InvoiceAsync(order.Id, order.Net, ct)
and can't see
Invoice

or Billing's tables, because the compiler stops it. Billing can change its tax rule or schema without touching Ordering. Both modules still share one process and one database, so a single transaction across them stays possible; with a monolith, Fowler notes, "you can update a bunch of things together in a single transaction". If Billing ever becomes a service, the seam already exists. Keep the contract coarse, though: Lewis and Fowler warn that "a good in-process interface is usually not a good service interface."

rows.text: Fowler: "The majority of software systems should be built as a single monolithic application."
It scales out with many instances behind a load balancer; it just can't scale one part alone
Starting with services avoids a rewrite
Early boundaries are often wrong, and moving them between services is much harder
Services give you modularity for free
They make boundaries firmer, but wrong boundaries become a handicap
Facebook and Etsy deliver large monoliths continuously

blocks.title: Splitting doesn't fix a tangled monolith

content.text: Fowler is explicit: "You cannot assume that you can take an arbitrary system and break it into microservices." Most systems acquire too many dependencies between modules, and the gradual migrations he heard of that worked "required a relatively good modular design to start with." Split a tangled monolith and you get a tangled distributed system, which a later article in this path covers.

blocks.title: Let the compiler guard the boundaries

content.text: Put each module in its own project, make everything
internal
except its contract, and register it with one call such as
AddBilling()
. A reference from Ordering to Billing's tables then fails to compile instead of slipping through review.

Fowler lists the complexity that pushes teams toward microservices: large teams, multi-tenancy, many user interaction models, business functions that must evolve independently, and scaling. The biggest is sheer size, a monolith "too big to modify and deploy." Not everyone agrees on starting with a monolith; Fowler's own view is that you shouldn't start with microservices unless the team has reasonable experience building them.
How to apply it in your project

items.title: Write down why you want services

content.text: List the concrete pain each split would solve. If the answer is "it's modern" or "it scales", a monolith behind a load balancer already covers it.
One project per module,
internal
by default, and each module owns its own tables. No module reads another module's tables.
Design each public interface as if it might become remote one day: few calls, whole requests and results, no entities leaking out.

items.title: Split when a specific pain appears

content.text: When one module needs its own release cadence, team or scaling, peel it off at the edge, the gradual route Fowler describes, and keep the rest together.
Key takeaways

items.text: Microservices are a trade-off with a real premium in distribution, consistency and operations, not a modern default.
A monolith scales out behind a load balancer; what it can't do is scale one part on its own.
Service boundaries are hardest to get right early, and much harder to move once they're remote.
Firm module boundaries are possible inside a monolith with discipline, and they're what makes a later split possible.
Split when a specific complexity demands it, starting from a modular monolith, not from a diagram.
